title: Microburst Queueing & Attention Oscillation — Case Study
body:
Purpose and short summary:
This is an exploratory write-up for a weird class of p99 spikes we saw on the nightly load test for long-context chat workloads (seq=4096). Symptoms: short microburst windows (~100–300ms) where requests pile, kernel handoff thrashes, and serving runtime switches between FlashAttention and a paged-attn fallback rapidly, producing 200–400ms p99 blips on otherwise smooth latencies. This doc collects traces, hypotheses, quick repro steps, numbers, and next-step remediation ideas.

Context and why this matters:
- Customer-facing SLA requires 95th/99th percentile stability at tail latencies; microbursts that self-amplify via queueing cause visible service degradation and retries.
- The runtime can pick multiple attention execution modes (FlashAttention fused kernels, paged-attention for very long sequences, and a fused-ops path for fused QKV + MLP kernels). Rapid mode switching can be expensive (warmups, kernel loads, memory copies).

High-level hypothesis chain (working):
1) Small bursts of large-sequence requests temporarily exhaust a per-GPU kernel pool or scheduler token, causing some requests to be queued on the CPU-side scheduler.
2) The queueing delays increase active sequence lengths seen by the kernel classifier (it sees longer contiguous KV caches) and flips the runtime to take a paged-attn path (kernel switch).
3) Kernel switch triggers KV materialization and a fused-op compatibility check; some paths require additional workspace allocation and GPU memcpy from pinned buffers, which creates a short but high-latency window.
4) When load subsides the runtime flips back to FlashAttention, but the return path has cold kernel-launch overheads and synchronization points that further add jitter.

Quick evidence snippets (from perf traces):
- Timeline excerpt (flattened trace ids):
  - t=0ms request A (seq=4096) — dispatched to worker-2, kernel=FlashAttention v1.3
  - t=12ms request B (seq=4096) — queued (scheduler token exhausted), pinned to worker-2
  - t=110ms scheduler: swap kernel->paged-attn for worker-2 (decision event), allocate extra 96MB workspace
  - t=128ms queued requests start executing on paged-attn (kernel launch + memcpy), p99 spike observed for B=~356ms
  - t=340ms kernel finishes, runtime attempts to revert to FlashAttention; additional 24ms stall observed during kernel unload
- Kernel selection metric log (sample window):
  - flash_hits: 67
  - paged_fallbacks: 9 (spikes correlate to microbursts)
  - fused_compat_check_failures: 3

Microbench numbers (isolated repro on dev GPU A100-80GB):
- Pure FlashAttention (warm) for batch=1 seq=4096: median=48ms, p99=62ms
- Paged-attn warm: median=130ms, p99=172ms
- Kernel switch overhead measured by injection test: 84±12ms (includes workspace alloc + memcpy + kernel load)
- Small-batch queueing backpressure: when more than 3 concurrent large seq requests hit, scheduler token queue length grows nonlinearly (observed slope change at concurrency=3 -> queue-length ~ O(c^2) until token freed)

Notes from kernel telemetry:
- There are ~2 places where allocations are racy under contention (allocator reports EAGAIN-like retries leading to extra memmove fallbacks).
- FlashAttention kernels use a different per-thread block policy; under certain occupancy patterns (lots of small origins followed by long ones) they underutilize SMs and trigger GPU-side serialization in our kernel launch path.

Repro steps (short):
1) Start local serving-runtime with feature flags: ATTENTION_MODE_AUTO=1, KERNEL_EAGER_LOAD=0, SCHED_TOKENS=3
2) Run synthetic client that issues 6 concurrent seq=4096 requests spaced 8ms apart for a 30s window (script attached below).
3) Collect rt-trace and /metrics; inspect kernel selection events and memalloc histogram.

Attached test script (sketch, inlined here):
- client-run.sh: launch 6 parallel curl POSTs to /v1/chat/complete with prompt size scaled to generate seq=4096 final length; loop 50x with jitter (0–12ms).

Observations from controlled runs:
- If KERNEL_EAGER_LOAD=1 (force pre-loading both Flash and paged kernels at start), microburst spikes drop by ~60% (p99 reduces from 356ms -> 140ms in this pattern), but overall GPU memory pressure increases and our memory allocator experiences more fragmentation over a sustained 15min test.
- If SCHED_TOKENS increased to 6, queueing disappears (requests dispatched immediately) but tail latency increases modestly because higher concurrency pushes paged-attn into frequent usage; net p99 slightly worse for mixed traffic.

Hypotheses to test (next experimental batch):
- H1: Eager kernel load + cheap guard rails (per-worker memory reservation) will suppress kernel-switch overheads without causing fragmentation for realistic windows (15min). Test: run 1h soak with eager load + reserve 512MB per worker. Metrics: mem-frag events, kernel-switch-count, p99.
- H2: Scheduler token strategy is too coarse-grained. Replace with prioritized token where long-seq requests get dedicated token slots (prevent them from being pre-empted by many short ones). Test: simulate mixed traffic with 80% short 512 tokens, 20% long 4096 tokens.
- H3: Fused-ops compatibility path is overly strict under misaligned KV layouts. Relax some alignment checks and fallback earlier to FlashAttn compatible buffer layout. Risk: correctness/regression — use unit tests.

Short-term mitigations (practical):
- Enable KERNEL_EAGER_LOAD selectively for GPU classes where memory headroom>30% during the window (monitoring rule: free_mem_pct > 35%).
- Reduce SCHED_TOKEN aggression (increase to concurrency ceiling of 4) and implement soft-priority for long requests.
- Add lightweight kernel-switch cooldown (e.g., once a worker switches to paged-attn, require min_revert_interval=250ms before switching back). This prevents flip-flop oscillation.

Logs / admin notes (raw):
- "2025-11-04T03:12:47Z TRACE kernel_switch ev=to_paged worker=wk-07 alloc=98304KB reason=seq_long queued=4"
- "2025-11-04T03:12:48Z WARN mem_alloc retry=3 fallback=memmove_to_host id=0x7f03b..."
- "2025-11-04T03:13:11Z METRIC p99_latency=342ms window=30s test=long-seq-microburst-run-1"

Open questions / unknowns (to answer):
- Why exactly do allocator retries happen only during those windows? Is it fragmentation (we suspect yes) or an interference with other processes pinned to the GPU (rare but possible on shared nodes)? Need nvml snapshots.
- What is the exact cost composition of kernel_switch overhead? We need a microtrace that splits allocation, memcpy, kernel load, and any CPU-RT synchronization.
- Is there a hardware-specific behavior (observed more on A100-80GB than V100 in quick sampling)? Could be driver/kernel interplay. Run same script across instance types.

Action items and owners (quick):
- Priya: orchestrate 1h soak with eager kernel load + 512MB reserve on 3 node types (A100-80GB, A100-40GB, V100). Collect allocator and nvprof traces. Due: 2025-11-10.
- Jared: prototype prioritized scheduler tokens (long-request bias) and unit test fallback. Small PR + perf harness. Due: 2025-11-14.
- Evelyn: split kernel_switch trace into sub-steps using perf events (in-kernel timestamps) and post here. Due: 2025-11-07.

Quick notes-to-self (informal):
- "If eager load reduces spikes but memory frag gets worse after 30min — explore slab-based allocator to hold kernel workspace in a pooled manner rather than free/alloc churn."
- "Consider lightweight admission control that senses nav-estimated future load (predict 200ms horizon) and delays launching long sequences by random backoff to avoid synchronized bursts from clients."

Appendix: rough numeric summary (from 10 runs of the microburst script):
- baseline (auto kernel, tokens=3): p50=52ms, p95=88ms, p99=320ms, mean_q_len_peak=5.6
- eager_load=1 (no reserve): p50=58ms, p95=110ms, p99=140ms, mem_frag_events=12/10runs (avg)
- tokens=6: p50=120ms, p95=210ms, p99=370ms (higher overall due to more paged usage)

Concluding notes:
- This appears to be a combined scheduler + allocator + kernel-selection oscillation problem rather than a single kernel regression. Short-term we can mitigate with eager loading + cooldowns; longer-term fix is to rework kernel selection state machine to be hysteretic and to introduce a pooled workspace allocator to avoid fragmentation-induced retries.

TODO: create a small benchmark harness that simulates mixed short/long clients with realistic jitter and attach to CI nightly to detect regressions (see linked PR for harness).

End of notes.
